newsitem.title: USA: Aetna posts sharp loss in fourth quarter.
newsitem.headline: Aetna posts sharp loss in fourth quarter.

text.p: Aetna Inc. Wednesday reported bigger losses than expected in the fourth quarter due to restructuring costs, price pressures and a loss at its medical insurance unit.
In October, Aetna announced plans to slash 4,400 jobs and restructure its health care and retirement services units.

Aetna lost $107.1 million, or 80 cents a share, in the quarter, as one-time items reduced operating income by $280 million after taxes. These include $301 million in severance and facilities, and other charges in Aetna U.S. Healthcare that wiped out a $21.0 million gain.
A year ago, Aetna earned $175.7 million, or $1.53 a share.
But full-year profits soared to $651.0 million, or $4.74 a share, thanks to $85.9 million of net realised capital gains and $445.9 million from discontinued property-casualty operations.
In 1995, Aetna earned $251.7 million, or $2.21 a share, including $29.5 million of capital gains and $222 million of net losses from the discontinued property-casualty operations.
Revenues jumped 33 percent to $4.49 billion in the fourth quarter from $3.37 billion in the 1995 period. They rose to $9.29 billion from $7.51 billion for the year.

"Aetna has reinvented itself as a new, leaner enterprise, composed of three complementary businesses linked in a common focus on growth and shareholder value," said Ronald Compton, chairman of the Hartford, Conn.-based company.
"Aetna U.S. Healthcare is rapidly combining the strengths of its two predecessors and is right on schedule in our mission to create the nation's premier health care company."
Including the unusual items, Aetna U.S. Healthcare had a net operating loss of $214.1 million in the fourth quarter.
Aetna's stock fell $4.375 to $78 on the New York Stock Exchange as the disappointing results gave investors a reason to take profits after the stock's recent strength.
"Medical cost inflation was evident," Bear Stearns analyst Gary Frazier said.
Costs were up throughout the year because of depressed premium rate increases and rising medical costs, Salomon Brothers analyst Robert Hoehn said in a research report.
The most prominent elements of the rise in fourth-quarter medical costs were the impact of mandatory 48-hour maternity stays and pharmacy costs, Hoehn said in the report.
Frazier said the results also were hurt by the pricing in Aetna's medical business, which was flat compared with last quarter and below analysts' expectations.
Total assets under management rose 20 percent to $32.0 billion as of Dec. 31.

Aetna International, which sells life and health insurance and financial services in emerging markets, saw fourth-quarter operating earnings rise to $27.1 million from $24.5 million a year ago. The improvement was driven by strong business growth in established markets, particularly Taiwan and Chile.

Large Case Pensions, which manages a variety of retirement and other savings products for defined benefit and defined contribution plan customers, reported fourth-quarter operating earnings of $51.3 million, up from $21.0 million a year ago. Fourth-quarter 1996 earnings include a $21.0 million after-tax benefit from a reduction in discontinued product reserves.
Aetna said it expects a new Brazilian joint venture to boost earnings by the end of the year.
Aetna this week said it will invest and initial $300 million to acquire up to 49 percent of a joint venture with Sul America Seguros, Brazil's largest insurance company.
